explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Luke says Jesus "went out to the mountain to pray." Right after a tense moment with people who were filled with rage, He heads off to talk with His Father. I think that tells you where He turns first.
Rest sounds reasonable, baker, because I'd want a nap after a day like that. But Luke says Jesus went out to the mountain to pray. That's the reason the text gives, so that's the one we keep.

Good guess, baker, because mountains and fasting show up together in a lot of stories. Not in this one, though. Luke says Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and fasting isn't mentioned in this passage.
Not quite, baker. Luke doesn't say a quick prayer. He says Jesus "spent the night in prayer to God." That's a whole night, not a short while.
Right, baker. Luke says Jesus "spent the night in prayer to God." That's the whole night, and daylight comes in the very next verse. A short while it was not.
That's the number, baker. Luke says Jesus "chose twelve of them." He picks them out of the larger group of disciples, and the names come right after.
Seven is a nice number, baker, but it's not this one. Luke says Jesus chose twelve of His disciples. Count the names in the list and you'll see twelve of them.
Three would make for a small team, baker. Luke says Jesus chose twelve of the disciples. The list that follows has twelve names, so all of them fit.
That's it, baker. Luke says Jesus chose twelve "whom He also designated as apostles." So these twelve get a name of their own, picked by Jesus Himself.
Prophets is a real title in the Bible, baker, but it's not the one here. Luke says Jesus designated the twelve as apostles. That's the word to remember for this group.
Elders is a title you'll find elsewhere in Scripture, baker, but not in this verse. Luke says Jesus designated the twelve He chose as apostles. That's the title for this team.
Yes, baker. Luke says "Simon, whom He named Peter." Jesus is the One who gives him the name. His brother Andrew comes right after him in the list.
Stephen is a good name, baker, but it's not on this list. Luke says Simon is the one "whom He named Peter." So Peter is the new name Jesus gives him.
Silas starts with an S like Simon, so I see how it slipped in. But he isn't in this list of twelve. Luke says Jesus named Simon Peter.
That's him, baker. Luke lists "Simon called the Zealot." That tag is how you tell him apart from the other Simon, the one Jesus named Peter. Two Simons on one team needs a little help.
Tanner sounds like a real name tag, baker, but it's not what Luke gives. He lists "Simon called the Zealot." That's the label that sets him apart from the Simon named Peter.
No, baker, that's not on this list. Luke says "Simon called the Zealot." The Zealot tag tells him apart from Simon Peter, since the two share a first name.

That's what the text says, baker. Luke ends the list with “…Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.” This one is heavy to read, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit. The writer tells us this about him right there in the list.

Close to the end of the list, but not the right label. Luke says Judas Iscariot "became a traitor." Tax collector isn't what the text says about him here. It's a heavy line, so take your time with it.

Fisherman isn't what Luke says about him, baker. Here the text says Judas Iscariot "became a traitor." That's a heavy thing to find at the end of a list of names, so I'll keep it simple and let the verse speak.

explanations.answer: To hear Him and be healed
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Luke says "They had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases." They came for His words and for His healing, and they got both.
The apostles were just chosen, so I see why you'd pick that. But Luke gives a different reason. The crowd "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases."

That was the mood back in the Sabbath scene, baker, with those leaders talking among themselves. But here Luke says the people "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases." That's the reason the text gives for this crowd.
That's right, baker. Luke says "those troubled by unclean spirits were healed." It's right there next to the diseases. Nobody who came was turned away.
Careful here, baker, because this one is true. Luke says "those troubled by unclean spirits were healed." The text says they were healed, so that's the answer.
That's the word, baker. Luke says "The entire crowd was trying to touch Him." They weren't only watching from a distance, they were reaching for Him.
Seeing Him would be a fine reason to come, baker, but it's not the word Luke uses. He says the entire crowd was trying to touch Jesus. They wanted to reach Him.
Follow is a good Bible word, baker, but it's not in this verse. Luke says "The entire crowd was trying to touch Him." That's the word that fits the blank.

explanations.answer: Power from Him was healing every one of them
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. Luke says they were trying to touch Him "because power was coming from Him and healing them all." The power was coming from Jesus, and the healing reached them all.

explanations.answer: They hoped He would pick them as apostles too
explanations.explanation: The twelve were just chosen, so it's a fair thought, baker. But Luke never says the crowd was hoping for that. He gives the reason: "power was coming from Him and healing them all."

explanations.answer: They believed it would keep away future sickness
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, baker, but Luke doesn't say that. He doesn't tell us what the people believed about the future. He says they tried to touch Him "because power was coming from Him and healing them all."
